content:
While Apple has tried to keep Jony Ive at arm's length from its lawsuit against OpenAI, the company may not be able to prevent its former design chief from being dragged into the dispute. Here's why.

OpenAI has a chance to put Apple in a very awkward position.

In its lawsuit accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets, Apple has conspicuously avoided mentioning Jony Ive. His company, io Products, partnered with OpenAI on the core hardware product at the centre of Apple's allegations.

One line in the complaint says "OpenAI and its confederates have engaged in organised, institutional misconduct," and includes io, but only describes it as "an enterprise co-founded by Mr. Tang and other former Apple executives." Otherwise, the complaint doesn't name Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executives—only Tang Tan and Chang Liu, who are directly accused of wrongdoing.

While it's still too early to say whether Ive might be called to testify, it is a possibility—especially if OpenAI decides to use him to make Apple uncomfortable or embarrassed.

That would put Apple in an unusually delicate position. Since leaving in 2019, Ive has publicly maintained a respectful stance toward Apple, with his public appearances and interviews carefully choreographed.

These have included appearances alongside Laurene Powell Jobs and ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive personally wrote a letter for the archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" project, reflecting on his time working with Jobs.

Apple, for its part, appears to have reciprocated the goodwill, carefully adjusting its stance on several controversial decisions made during his tenure, including the MacBook butterfly keyboard. Its attempt to keep Ive at a distance from the lawsuit fits the same approach.

But once the case enters discovery, Apple doesn't have full control over who gets pulled in. Given Ive's role in founding io Products and overseeing the hardware project in question, OpenAI could argue he has relevant knowledge about how the product was developed, what information the team had access to, and whether any Apple trade secrets were used.

Apple could then face the awkward prospect of questioning Ive on the stand, challenging his testimony, or trying to undermine the credibility of the executive who shaped some of the company's most iconic products.

This wouldn't be Ive's first time testifying in a lawsuit involving Apple. In 2012, he was deposed during Apple's patent battle with Samsung, answering questions about Apple's design process and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

However, testifying for the opposing side could damage the carefully maintained relationship he's had with Apple—and could even cause friction with OpenAI if Ive feels he's been unnecessarily pulled into the dispute to give his former employer an edge.

Do you think Jony Ive will be pulled into this lawsuit? Let us know in the comments.
